en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who was a bearer of the burden of the tradition of the venerable teacher Prabhākara.
Adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and the gloss on difficult passages (*viṣamasthala-ṭippaṇī*),
this is now the first chapter of the *Aṅgapārāyaṇa*, dedicated to the definition of the auxiliary factors that provide direct assistance (*sannipatyopakāraka-aṅga*).
The declaration of the subject matter:

In order to dispel doubts concerning the possible variations in interpretation regarding the constituent parts [of the treatise], I shall expound the supreme and profound intent of my teacher Prabhākara. (1)
The fourfold nature of the auxiliaries (*aṅga*):
here, the group of auxiliaries is fourfold—consisting of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), substance (*dravya*), and the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).
Among these, even that which consists of the meaning of the verbal root is twofold: that which assists by direct contact (*sannipatyopakāraka*) and...
And there is that which assists from a distance;
thus, there are four types of cooperative conditions.
Among these, the cooperative condition through conjunction is of four kinds.
Due to the distinctions of production, acquisition, transformation, and refinement as the objects to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
[the means] take the form of kneading, milking, melting, sprinkling, and so forth, respectively. Among these, through kneading, a lump that did not previously exist is produced.
Only milk is obtained through milking;
by melting it, one sets aside its previous solid state, and another liquid state arises as clarified butter (*ājya*).
For clarified butter (*ājya*), being earthen (*pārthiva*) and possessing fragrance, is by its very nature a solid form that becomes liquid through contact with fire.

Regarding this, the Blessed Kāśyapa said: “The liquidity of earthen substances such as ghee (*sarpiḥ*), lac (*jatu*), and beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*) due to contact with fire is a commonality with water” (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.6).

Likewise, it has been stated by the Grammarians (*śābdika*): “Because of the use of the *cvipratyaya* suffix in the expression ‘clarified butter becomes liquid through contact with fire’ [it is understood to be earthy].”

But sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) does not bestow a new state upon a substance by means of the destruction of its prior state; for there is a verse on this point: "By the abandonment of a prior state and the assumption of another state, they call *vikāra* (modification) a *saṃskāra* (refinement); [but] it is merely the arising of an excellence. (Verse 2)
Thus ends the definition of the factors that function through conjunction.
But what, then, is the defining characteristic of these four in their capacity as cooperative conditions through conjunction?
That which produces a result depending on the injunction regarding a *kāraka* is an "accessory by direct contact" (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*).
For example, bathing for the agent.
1380. Regarding the object (*karman*), [examples include] threshing and so forth;
regarding the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the bringing of curd and so forth—these are to be inferred.
This is the objection according to the Bhaṭṭa school.
In that regard, concerning the sentences containing subsidiaries that assist through conjunction (*sannipatyopakāraka*), some accept them as separate injunctions (*vidhi*).

For they think: "If separate injunctions were not accepted here, then, due to the principle of qualification by the primary context (*adhikṛtādhikāra*), the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgatva*) for acts such as husking (*avaghāta*) would not exist."
Nor is subsidiary status established through a connection with a substance by virtue of a connection with the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) under the heading of the subject matter at hand,
because words such as "rice" (*vrīhi*) denote the generic form (*ākṛti*).
Even though the word for the genus has the individual instances as its indirect meaning (*lakṣaṇārtha*) due to their proximity to the action to be accomplished, [it does not denote the substance].
Nevertheless, only the individual instance (*vyakti*) is indicated, not an individual instance connected with a previously unknown specific [efficacy].

Nor can there be a connection with the *apūrva* by virtue of indicating that individual instance which is the means to the *apūrva*, as in the case of the *Āgneyī* [verse], on the grounds of its being the subject under discussion.
Even though, according to the principle of the *āgneyī* [mantras], there is an inclusion of the proximate individuals, nevertheless,
those individuals are cognized by their very nature alone, through the exclusion of individuals not under discussion,
and not by virtue of being the means for accomplishing a specific *apūrva*.
Because that intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is something to be defined (*lākṣaṇika*),
and there is no reason for a "definition of the defined" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).
For instance, the individual (*vyakti*) is defined by the genus (*jāti*).
Furthermore, because there is no basis for it, the definition-by-indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*)— whereby a specific means [of accomplishment] would be indicated by the individual instance—

is incorrect. For this very reason, in the case of the injunction “With the *Āgneyī* verse he worships the *Āgnīdhra* altar” (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 3.1.6), even though the context (*prakaraṇa*) is present,
the *Āgnīdhra* is not worshipped with a different verse.

For this very reason, there is no contradiction regarding the application of what has already been applied (*viniyuktaviniyoga*) in that case; for [the mantra] is not applied to the attendance upon the *Āgnīdhra* priest by virtue of being a means for accomplishing some other purpose. And thus, since threshing and the like are connected with the ritual action only in their own essential form (*svarūpamātra*), the connection with a specific transcendental result (*apūrva*) is not established.
It is like the restriction of speech at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice.
Just as the restriction of speech, due to its connection with its own intermediate apūrva, does not enter into the apūrva of the primary entitlement (*adhikāra*),
so too should it be with threshing and other such acts.

Consequently, prior to the qualified injunction (*adhikāra-apūrva*), threshing and other such acts would not possess the status of being subsidiaries (*aṅga*). And if they were not subsidiaries, there would be no impulsion (*prayukti*) for them, and thus the performance of threshing and the rest would not occur.
Therefore, one must accept that the original injunction (*utpatti-niyoga*) applies to threshing and the like.
Indeed, when that [result] is resorted to, since its performance is untenable due to the absence of an entitlement (adhikāra), and an entitled person must therefore be postulated,
it follows that the very same person entitled to the primary apūrva is also entitled to the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and so forth.
"The means [is not established] as a subordinate member because it does not have the nature of being that which is to be attained"—this is the objection. The refutation of that is as follows:
the venerable teacher does not accept this.
Regarding this, it was said: "You are ignorant of the objects to be enjoined," in the commentary on Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3.
In the case of threshing and similar acts, the removal of husks and chaff is seen both from the word itself and from the inherent nature of the thing.
In rites such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and others, an unseen effect (adṛṣṭa) is accepted precisely because of the verbal testimony;
if, in that context, another effect in the form of an injunction (niyoga) were also assumed, then two effects would not be construed within a single sentence.
And this [result] cannot be of such a nature as heaven and so forth,
because it is construed as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
Furthermore, the removal of the husks and chaff and so forth is not a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), because it is the fruit of the action;
only that which is the fruit of the injunction (*niyoga*) itself undergoes the status of being a qualification of the person to be enjoined.
For the person to be impelled (niyojya), being qualified by the goal, is able to understand only that as the task (kārya) which accomplishes his very goal; thus,
the accomplishment of the qualification of the person to be impelled is determined.

And that which is the fruit of an action does not come about through the mandate; therefore, one who possesses such a fruit does not attain the status of a person to be enjoined (*niyojyatā*) with respect to the mandate.
Nor is it logical to abandon an action such as the removal of perceived chaff and husks, precisely because that [action] has been perceived.
But surely, since an injunction (*niyoga*) is also perceived by virtue of the employment of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth which denote an injunction, the fault is equal for both sides.
It is said:
when an injunction is present, it is proper to understand that very injunction as it is being understood;
in that case, if the object were not included within its scope, [the injunction would be frustrated].
In that case, there would be a different injunction;
yet threshing and so forth enter into the scope of the original context, because they are connected with the rice and other materials intended for that purpose.
The words *avahanti* (he threshes) and so forth denote threshing and other such acts precisely as being subordinate to the injunction (*niyoga*) within the context of what is proximate (*sannihita*),
because those acts, being of such a nature, are taught as having the relationship of action and factor (*kriyā-kāraka-bhāva*).
If there were a connection with rice (*vrīhi*) and the like while they remained merely in their own form (*svarūpa-mātra*), [then that would not be the case].

In that case, there would be no connection with its specific qualification; rather, it is the [grain] presented by words such as *vrīhi*— which denote a particular means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) belonging to that [ritual]— that is connected with threshing and so forth,
not the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone.
And thus, by the very fact of such instruction, threshing and other such acts are established even in the case of barley, since there is no difference in their status as means to the end.
For this very reason, threshing and the like are enjoined precisely because they have not been previously obtained as means for fulfilling the mandate (*niyoga*).
The restriction, however, serves a specific purpose:

if acts such as threshing were not enjoined as constituent parts of the primary injunction (*niyoga*), then even methods such as tearing with the fingernails would be implied for the sake of merely preparing the *puroḍāśa* cake.
However, when acts such as threshing are enjoined as constituent parts of the *niyoga*,
they are necessarily implied because the fulfillment of the *niyoga* is impossible without them;
yet, their status as constituent parts of the *niyoga* is not established even in the alternative case [of the opponent's view].
Since *niyoga* (the mandate) is something not known through ordinary worldly experience, its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) cannot be understood from anything other than the word itself;
and because acts such as *avaghāta* (threshing) are auxiliaries of the *niyoga*,
their connection with the *niyoga* is restated by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth regarding that which has already been established.
The doubt regarding whether threshing and the like are the objects of the injunction, and its refutation:
Now, if threshing and the like have a connection with the injunction, how then can it be said that they are not the objects of the injunction?
It is stated as follows: It is not merely the state of being connected to an injunction that is expressed;
rather, that for which the accomplishment of the injunction itself is the primary effect is the object (*viṣaya*).
And since threshing and other such acts produce intermediate effects such as the removal of husks and chaff, they do not constitute the objects of the injunction.
Thus it is established that [the means] are not the object of the mandate (niyoga),
whereas acts such as threshing are indeed subsidiary (aṅga) because they are employed for the sake of accomplishing the mandate.

As it has been said: "That which is employed for the sake of accomplishing that [niyoga] is designated as 'to be enjoined' (vidheya)"; such is the convention in the Tantra [Sūtra 2, Vṛtti-Ṭīkā, p. 39].

Thus, it is established that threshing and other such acts are auxiliary to the niyoga solely by virtue of their proximity, reinforced by the recognition of the niyoga itself, and not through the mediation of the syntactical connection of word-meanings.
Furthermore, for those who maintain that entry [into the ritual] occurs by way of the syntactical connection of the word-meanings (*padārthānvaya*),

there is no distinction between the *sāptadaśya* (the number seventeen) taught in a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) and the *pāñcadaśya* (the number fifteen) taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), since both enter [the rite] by way of their connection with the *sāmidhenī* verses.
Both [the fifteen-fold and the seventeen-fold sets] would be included within the context itself, and there would be an option between them;
for if that which is studied within the context were grasped merely by its proximity, then the fifteen-fold set would enter into the governing injunction more quickly.
Once that [the *sāmidhenī* verses] has been established, the requirement of seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) cannot enter into it because it would contradict its specific qualification;
therefore, its application occurs only in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
If, on the basis of proximity, it were to enter into the primary injunction of qualification, [it would be untenable].
In that case, how is there an inclusion of the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa*-wood) and other such qualities, which are taught as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*)?
It is said: since the *juhū* (ladle) and others have an invariable connection with the sacrifice, their connection with the sacrifice is established by way of that [connection with the ladle].
And because the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth is connected only to those things— such as the *juhū* ladle— that are themselves connected to that [sacrifice],
for this very reason, "Gold is to be worn" (*hiraṇyaṃ bhāryam*) is the object of an independent injunctive mandate (*adhikāraniyoga*), since gold does not invariably relate to the sacrifice.
Furthermore, for those who maintain that because it would result in meaninglessness if there were a connection with the intrinsic natures of the word-meanings,
the connection with the cognizer must be preceded by a connection with the state of their mutual relation—
how can this even be possible for them?
"It must not be purposeless"—
if you argue this on the grounds that it is a Vedic statement?
It has not been decreed by the King that the Veda must not be purposeless.
Let there be no pointlessness for that [word] whose meaning is understood; however,
the meaningfulness of a word whose meaning is not ascertained is merely a product of imagination.

Since meaningfulness exists even by taking another alternative as a basis, it is better to accept its status as a subordinate element of the injunction (*niyoga*) by virtue of proximity (*sannidhāna*). Those learned in the theory of sentences (*vākya-vidaḥ*) maintain that proximity is also a cause for establishing a relationship.
Furthermore, a relationship cannot exist without a distinction between the subordinate and the principal;
and in that regard, since "an effect does not exist for the sake of another," the injunction (*niyoga*) alone is the principal, while threshing and other such acts are merely subsidiaries.
Regarding the doubt and its resolution concerning proximity (*sannidhāna*):

if the connection with the injunction were based on purposelessness (*ānarthakya*), then the rule “the third triplet is the *paryāsa*” would not find application even within the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
For the connection with a sacrifice is said to be internal within the *paryāsa* section;
therefore, even when there is a connection merely with the ritual items (*padārtha*) therein, there is no pointlessness.

Likewise, in the case of the injunction regarding the properties of the ladles—“The ladles are made of gold” (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 8.5.29)—there is no pointlessness, because the ladles have an invariable connection with the sacrifice.
There would be no connection with the subject matter under discussion. Furthermore, since a connection with the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) has been accepted in order to avoid meaninglessness,
why is a connection with the proximate *apūrva* not resorted to?
If proximity were not a cause [for restriction],
then the rule "he gathers grass for the fire" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 3.4.3) would not be restricted to the Agnihotra sacrifice alone.
Alternatively, if there is acceptance of the fires and other elements connected to that *apūrva* on account of a specific proximity, [then the restriction holds].
In that case, let there simply be a connection with that apūrva due to a specific proximity;
what is the use of resorting to an indirect succession?
Just as in the case of the expression of a related meaning through the relation of action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva).
Likewise, in common worldly usage, the relationship between a purpose and that which serves it is well-established;
for rice and such things cannot themselves be understood as the ultimate purpose.
Therefore, setting those aside, the connection by way of the relationship between purpose and that which serves it is with the apūrva alone.
Regarding the intermediate apūrva (intermediate transcendental result), there is a doubt and its refutation:

In the view of those who maintain that there are intermediate apūrvas in acts such as threshing, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)— in the injunction “one threshes with the two sprinkled pestle and mortar”— would be prompted by an intermediate apūrva, just like the restriction of silence (*vāṅniyama*) at the Dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice.
Furthermore, there would be a restriction of speech as in the case of the *traidhātavīyā* sacrifice;
yet, in the case of rice-grains split by the nails, there should be no sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*),
because the specific form that motivates it is not present there.
Nor should it be said that the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the entitlement is the motivator solely by way of the effects such as the removal of husks and chaff;
for if that were so, the same would follow even in the case of the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*).
Furthermore, in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] as well, there exists an effect consisting in the production of what is required by the sacrifice.
The Jyotiṣṭoma alone should be the motivator for the restriction of speech;
consequently, it would also apply to the Traidhātavīyā sacrifice, which brings about the status of being initiated (*dīkṣita*).
Now, [one might object]: "If intermediate injunctions (*avāntara-vidhi*) are not accepted in the case of threshing and other such acts..."

How then is it that the Commentator accepts an intermediate injunction (*antarvidhi*) specifically regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), stating: "And that which is not enjoined does not become a subsidiary" (Śābarabhāṣya, Adhikaraṇa 3, Pāda 4, Adhikaraṇa 13)? It is said in reply:
An intermediate injunction is accepted in the case of a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) and in the prohibition of speaking untruth (*anṛtavādapratiṣedha*).
Because subsidiariness (aṅgatva) is untenable apart from that [assistance];
since actions are momentary by their very nature,
they do not persist at the time when the assistance is produced, and thus subsidiariness is not possible.
We shall explain this very point here.

For this reason, regarding the recitation of the *jajjabhyamāna-mantra*, which provides a direct auxiliary benefit (*sannipatyopakārin*), the author of the Bhāṣya states: "The mention of human effort is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
This is because where there exists an intermediate injunction (*avāntara-vidhi*), [the effort is already established].
In that context, the mention of human effort is not a mere restatement;
for it is precisely that intermediate apūrva which is denoted by the optative suffix (liṅ) and other such markers as something to be accomplished.
Furthermore, since it is not possible to express an effect whose nature is delimited by an action without expressing the human effort that consists in that action,
it is logical to express the human effort consisting in that action for that purpose; thus,
human effort is not unintended.

Thus, by virtue of the proximity of the scriptural mention reinforced by the injunction and the recognition [of the same act], threshing and other such acts— having been understood as being connected with the injunctive requirements of the primary mandate through words such as "threshes" (avahanti)—
become subordinate to those [grains] insofar as they enter into a relationship of action and factor with the rice and other materials already connected to that mandate.
The statement regarding the application of the *śruti* and other means according to our own view:
What, then, is the authority for the threshing being subsidiary to the rice and so forth?
We say it is the *kārya* (the purpose).
For instance: an effect does not exist for the sake of something else, precisely because it is an effect.
Therefore, whatever is connected with an effect, [is for the sake of that effect].
That much is for that purpose;
and furthermore, whatever is connected with that which has been made subservient to the effect,
with that too there exists a relationship of probandum and probans.
That too is for that very purpose,
because there is no evidence for something that has attained subservience to one effect to have subservience to another;
in this way, the relationship of subsidiary and principal is to be understood in all cases.
If the understanding of the purpose [of a mantra] arises solely from its being an effect [of a ritual act],
then how can *śruti* and the other means of application (*viniyoga-kāraṇa*) function as causes of application? [They do so] by providing the specific means [through which the mantra operates].
And a subordinate (śeṣa) attains the status of being subordinate to the principal (śeṣin) by virtue of performing a specific function for it,
and not otherwise;
for it is impossible for that which accomplishes nothing to be subordinate.

In this regard, the scriptural text “one threshes the rice” (*vrīhīnavahanti*), being in the accusative case, presents the removal of husks and chaff from the rice and so forth as the objective realized by the action expressed in grammatical coordination; it thus restates the fact that [the threshing] is an instrument for the mandate (*niyoga*).
It does not, however, state through the accusative alone that the rice and so forth are the primary objects (*śeṣin*) and that the threshing is the subordinate element (*śeṣa*).
Because there is deviation in cases such as "he gives a cow" (*gāṃ dadāti*),

that which is invariably present everywhere— the state of being a recipient of the fruit produced by the action— is what must be expressed by the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*), not the state of being the primary object (*śeṣitā*).
Because it would be inconstant;
only that factor which is the recipient of the fruit produced by the action is the *karma*,
and that is something desired.
Because of the utility of what has been or will be;
and because some things are not desired, due to their lack of utility.

By this very distinction, there are two sūtras of the Blessed Pāṇini: "The object most desired by the agent is the *karman*" (Pāṇini 1.4.49), and "Likewise, that which is not desired but is connected in the same way [is also *karman*]" (Pāṇini 1.4.50).
This is according to those whose view is that the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is solely the residual relation (*śeṣa*).
In their view, the statement “gold is to be worn” would be merely a ritual duty (*kratudharma*).
For it is logical that [an injunction] should enter into a qualification consistent with what is heard in scripture,
rather than the postulation of an independent qualification.
Because it would follow that there is an abandonment of the understood remainder of the gold;
however, if the meaning of the word is the possession of the fruit produced by the action,
there is no loss of what was heard.
Since an independent agent is understood [from the verbal suffix], it is logical to postulate an entitlement (*adhikāra*) that serves as its cause.

Because there is no recognition of the previously mentioned injunction (*niyoga*), and since another injunction remains, the postulation of an entitlement—just like the postulation of an entitlement for the Prajāpati-vows—is what is intended.
This is the illustration of the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

In the case of bathing and other such acts, by reflecting on the inherent nature of the things involved, one accepts through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that their effect consists in the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent.
Therefore, by virtue of this capacity, bathing and the rest possess the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatā*) to the agent.
And the indicative mark (liṅga) is merely capacity,
not solely the capacity for denotation.
An example of a sentence (vākya) follows.

In passages such as "He offers while stepping forward" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.6.1), it is understood from the sentence (*vākya*) that the act of stepping forward is to be performed as part of the oblation;
thus, this application (*viniyoga*) is established by the sentence.
However, for those elements that provide direct assistance (*sannipatyopakāraka*), application by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not possible.
For those [elements] for which context establishes the door [of application],
their application is dependent upon context.
This is the definition of context.
The *prakaraṇa* (context) is the expectancy for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*).
And by that [expectancy], the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*), which constitutes the effect, is postulated.
Nor is this [assistance] the door for that which provides direct assistance (*sannipattyopakārin*).
There is no application of those [mantras] by way of context (*prakaraṇa*).

As for place (*sthāna*) and name (*samākhyā*), they do not possess the power of application regarding those things that assist through direct contact (*sannipatyopakāraka*). Furthermore, even in the case of place and name, there is no capacity to infer a purpose with respect to those things that assist through direct contact.
There is no causality of application (*viniyoga*);

thus, for those factors that assist by direct contact (*sannipatyopakāraka*), there is a purposefulness toward the injunction (*niyoga*) by virtue of their denotation, and a purposefulness toward the constituent factors (*kāraka*) by virtue of their application (*viniyoga*).

And by way of "appropriation" (*upādāna*), there is the subservience (*aidamarthyam*) of the sprinkling and so forth to the sacrifice and other rites which have become the object of the mandate and its application;

for appropriation is indeed the implication of the mandate, and it is by that [appropriation] that the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) is established for the sprinkling and other such acts.
If the assistance to the instrument provided by the sprinkling and so forth were not present,
then by what other means could the cognition of the *niyoga* (the mandate) as connected with that [sprinkling] be established?

It is the *niyoga* itself, once apprehended as connected with that [sprinkling], which— postulating its own status as an assistant to the instrument— implies that the sprinkling has the purpose of serving the instrument.

The fact that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other such acts serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) is established precisely by that [injunction]. However, because of their application (*viniyoga*), they possess the status of being for the sake of the factors of action (*kāraka-idamarthya*). How, then, do they contribute to the assistance of the instrument (*karaṇopakārakatā*)?
By providing a series of effects, such as the removal of husks and chaff, they bring about a specific benefit for that which is to be assisted.
If this is so, then while acts such as *avaghāta* (threshing), which enter into the category of the *kāraka*, serve to assist the instrument (*karaṇa*) by imparting a specific form to its body,
acts such as the *prayāja* sacrifices produce an assistance that benefits the instrument without being distinct from it; thus, a single common assistance is not produced by all of them.
Consequently, it would not follow that there is a single mode of operation (*eketikartavyatā*) for all [auxiliaries].
It is replied:
because the establishment of the assistance depends upon the specific recipient of that assistance, the specific recipient is capable of generating the assistance.
That [the benefit] belongs to no other is understood from the application of threshing and so forth;
and thus it is established that even threshing and the like produce a contributory benefit (*karaṇopakāra*) together with the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
This concludes the removal of the doubt regarding whether the directly-contributing (*sannipāti*) rites might instead be merely indirectly-contributing (*ārādupakāraka*).
But why are acts such as *āvadhāta* (threshing) not accepted as being contributory (*upakāraka*) in the same way as the *prayāja* offerings?
Because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the same governing injunction (*niyoga*) pertaining to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
And it has been stated that a unity of the injunction is possible here by way of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the rice-grains belonging to that [sacrifice].

For if it were admitted that threshing and the like are equivalent to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, we shall explain that another originative injunction (*utpatti-niyoga*) would have to be resorted to.
On this point, there are these summary verses: "Arising by virtue of proximity, [the action] goes toward the *apūrva* of the primary rite. (1409)
Let not recognition be obstructed; [this is said] out of a desire to favor it. // 3 //
By means of words such as "avahanti" (threshes), which denote objects associated with an action to be accomplished,
their own meaning is expressed only as connected to the primary apūrva.

This being the case, for one who wishes to preserve their status as belonging to that [Veda], there must be a definition of the means of accomplishing the task expressed by words such as "rice" and so forth. (5)
Therefore, the relationship between action and its factors (kāraka) also has the means of accomplishment (sādhana) as its domain;
likewise, the status of being the primary object (śeṣibhāva) belongs to that very same [means], in accordance with the path of the direct Vedic statement (śruti).

Thus ends the first chapter, dedicated to the determination of the directly contributive auxiliary factors (*sannipatyopakāraka-aṅga*), within the *Aṅgapārāyaṇa* section of the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the Great Professor, the venerable Śrīmat Śālikanātha Miśra.

Now begins the second chapter of the *Aṅgapārāyaṇa*, dedicated to the determination of the indirectly contributive auxiliary factors (*ārādupakāraka-aṅga*). Herein is the formal proposition regarding the subject matter of the treatise.
The indirectly contributory (ārādupakāraka) is of two kinds: that which has an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭaprayojana) and that which has both seen and unseen purposes (dṛṣṭādṛṣṭaprayojana).
Among these, that with an unseen purpose is exemplified by such injunctions as "He offers the *samidh* oblations" (*samidho yajati*, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.6.1.1).

No specific purpose pertaining to the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is observed for this [term]. The view of certain authorities regarding its scope as an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) is as follows:

first, some maintain that these [auxiliaries] possess a qualification for those already qualified (*adhikṛtādhikāra*), in order to establish their status as subsidiaries (*aṅgatā*) with respect to the transcendental result of the context (*adhikārāpūrva*).
For they think as follows: "In the case of the *samits* and other such [subsidiary rites], injunctions regarding production (*utpatti-niyoga*) are accepted without dispute.
Furthermore, an injunction is never expressed without an agent to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
If that were not so, there would be no need to postulate an agent to be enjoined in the case of the Viśvajit and other such [independent sacrifices]."
And in that case, when a person to be enjoined (niyojya) must be postulated, one must either postulate an attachment (*anuṣaṅga*) of the word denoting the fruit,
or postulate an eligible person (*adhikārī*) according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice.
In that case, the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) regarding the *apūrva* of the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is not fulfilled;
however, when there exists an entitled person (*adhikārī*) with reference to the supreme *apūrva*, the relationship between the means and the end (*upāya-upeyabhāva*) is understood.
For otherwise, the relationship between the qualified person and the qualification would not be logically tenable;
for he whose goal is the supreme apūrva is the one qualified for the supreme apūrva.

Therefore, just as in such injunctions as “One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa,” there exists a relationship of means and end between heaven and the sacrifice— with the qualified person (adhikārī) being one who desires heaven and is characterized by the heaven to be achieved— so too here exists such a relationship between the *samit* and other subsidiary acts and the ultimate transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*). In that regard, according to the principle that “an effect is not for the sake of another [without serving its own purpose],” it is determined that the *samit* and other acts serve the purpose of the primary injunction of qualification (*adhikāraniyoga*).
This is what is called "the grasping of the grasper.

In that regard, since the supreme *apūrva* is already occupied by the instrumental factors such as the *āgneya* sacrifice which are taught as originating [in the primary injunction], it is impossible for these [subsidiary acts] to serve its purpose through any other mode; therefore, their connection is only as *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance).
This is the refutation of that [position].
The Prābhākaras maintain that this is untenable.

For instance: if it is maintained that every *niyoga* (injunction) must be expressed as connected with a *niyojya* (the person to be impelled), then even the originative injunctions (*utpatti-niyoga*) for the specific sacrifices within the Rājasūya would necessarily possess a *adhikāra* (a qualified person entitled to perform them).

Consequently, the acts such as *videvana* (gambling) and others recited within the context of the *Abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice would be subsidiary to that very sacrifice by virtue of the context of the intermediate *apūrva* of the *Abhiṣecanīya*.

Now, it might be argued: "An injunction (*niyoga*) is not stated as being connected to an agent merely for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), but rather for the purpose of securing performance."

The *abhiṣecanīya* and other such rites obtain their performance solely through the impulsion (*prayukti*) of the supreme *apūrva*, because the supreme *apūrva* itself has those [rites] as its object; thus, when the sacrifices—which have become its objects—are employed by that [supreme *apūrva*] for the sake of its own accomplishment, the originating injunctions (*utpatti-niyoga*) whose objects are those [sacrifices] also achieve their fulfillment and do not require another person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) for their own accomplishment. Thus it is said.
In that case, the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, because their objects have already been assigned, would not require a separate qualification (*adhikāra*).
It might be argued: "The very assignment (*viniyoga*) of these [subordinate acts] is untenable without a qualification belonging to one who is already qualified.

That is incorrect; for, while they are first understood by the word as being connected to a qualification merely through their subservience to the primary injunction (*niyoga*), they are subsequently assigned as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

For instance— in the proximity of an injunction of qualification (adhikāravidhi), such [sentences] as "He offers the *samidhs*" (*samidho yajati*) are indeed transmitted as being themselves devoid of a qualification.

In that context, that very injunction of qualification, which serves as the primary purpose, is denoted by its own word as being connected with the *samit*-offerings and so forth— which are themselves not primary purposes but are devoid of a qualification.

Furthermore, the sentences concerning the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and so forth present the very forms of sacrifices qualified by their respective materials and deities; through mere presentation, they enter into syntactic connection with the injunctive mandate of the primary qualification (*adhikāraniyoga*).
And if this presentation were not taken into account, [the connection would be impossible].
In that case, there is a syntactic connection with the injunction regarding the qualification for the *samit* (fuel-stick) offering.

Furthermore, if proximity (*sannidhāna*) were not taken into account, then why would one postulate a qualification for the supreme *apūrva* (transcendental result) even in the case of the *samit* offerings and others?
Thus, when the subservience to the qualified person (*adhikāra-idamarthyam*) is established merely by proximity, there arises an expectancy as to how this comes about;
likewise, there is an inquiry as to how the *apūrva* of the qualification, which is itself that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is brought about.
Therefore, it is the very assistance to the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*) that is relied upon as their means (*dvāra*).
In that context, when there is an expression of the related meaning (anvitābhidhāna) by way of being for the sake of this [result], that is the grasping of the grasper;
and as for the conceptualization of those [means] by way of the assistance to the instrument, [that is the grasping of the grasped].
That itself is the application by context (*prakaraṇaviniyoga*).
[This concludes] the refutation of the doubt regarding the denial of intermediate apūrvas. But, in that case, have the intermediate apūrvas not been denied?
We do not deny this;

for although the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth are initially unable to convey a distinct *niyoga* (an injunction), they function as restatements (*anuvādaka*) of an already suspected injunctive authority (*adhikāra-niyoga*), as in such cases as "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*).

Nevertheless, since these momentary factors do not produce intermediate apūrvas with respect to the mandate of the primary qualification (adhikāra), their status as subsidiaries (aṅgatā) would not be tenable;

therefore, those intermediate apūrvas which must subsequently be resorted to in order to establish the status of being subsidiaries to the apūrva of the primary qualification are accepted as being denoted by the optative suffix (liṅ).
This has been demonstrated in the section concerning the restriction of speech during the Dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice (Mīmāṃsādarśana 9.1.2).
Now, we shall explain in this very context how the acceptance of intermediate apūrvas among these substrates occurs; and as for those intermediate apūrvas—
These [subsidiary acts], being constituent parts by virtue of the verbal injunction, are presented toward the *apūrva* of the primary qualification (*adhikārāpūrva*).
Regarding the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, there is the raising and refutation of the doubt concerning an intermediate *apūrva*.
[Objection: If that is so, then in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others, the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*) would not be prompted by an intermediate *apūrva*.

However, [one might argue that] it would follow that [the threshing] is prompted by that *apūrva*, just as in the case of the rule "one threshes with the mortar and pestle after they have been sprinkled. No;
for that [sprinkling] is for the purpose of accomplishing the essential form [of the implements], even though the intermediate *apūrvas* constitute subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the final *apūrva*.

Nevertheless, in those cases, the dharma consisting of vocal restraint and so forth serves solely for the sake of accomplishing their own specific forms (svarūpa), because it is understood that they are connected to the specific form of an intermediate apūrva related to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, as stated in the rule: "One should recite the invitatory verse at the *dīkṣaṇīyā*" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 20.4.10).
Nor is it appropriate to characterize them through a relationship of subsidiary and principal by abandoning their own specific forms.
For it is precisely the definition [of the object] that is [the purpose];
nor is there a lack of performance because the object is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*),
since the essential nature itself is established as being cognizable by nothing other than that.
Everything whose accomplishment is known solely through verbal testimony is *apūrva* (unseen).

However, in the case of acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*), since their accomplishment is ascertainable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), their essential form (*svarūpa*) is established even without the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
If [the act] were for the sake of its own essential form, the performance of the restrictive injunction (*niyamaniyoga*) would be illogical.

Thus, since the *prayāja* and other such rites have already been established as constituent parts (*aṅga*) by their own nature, there is no occasion for the postulation of a separate qualification (*adhikāra*).

In that very same manner, the intermediate operation (*avāntara-vyāpāra*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*) must be understood to exist within the originative injunctions (*utpatti-niyoga*) concerning the primary acts.
For he who does not accept that intermediate operation—
In that case, there would be no distinction of instruments in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices;
likewise, the properties of the Āgneya and other offerings would apply to the Upāṃśuyāja and others, because they would be prompted by the supreme apūrva.
Because there is no difference in their status as means for that [result].
However, a distinction is appropriate when there is a difference in intermediate operations;
otherwise, the *āgneya* sacrifice would possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatā*).
"Otherwise, [there would be no distinction] regarding the Upāṃśuyāja and other such rites.
Just as there is a fixed rule of dharma (*dharmavyavasthā*) whereby the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans], though both means of praise, function as means in different ways,
so too it is with the two Pārvaṇa-homas.
For this very reason, there is sublation (*bādha*) in the modified rites (*vikṛti*).

For the *saurya* sacrifice does not possess the same status as a means to the unseen potency (*apūrva*) as the *āgneya* does; thus, due to the absence of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) medium, there is sublation of the two *pārvaṇa-homas*.

Furthermore, those intermediate *apūrvas* which do not exist and are not described as being of the nature of means (*sādhana*) cannot be considered intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*); thus, all the aforementioned defects would follow.
For the status of being an intermediate operation consists in being the cause for the production of the final effect.
Otherwise, even exhaustion arising from agriculture would have to be considered an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) in the attainment of the crop, just like plowing.
[Objection: But if it were thus devoid of a specific qualification (*adhikāra*), there would be no extended application (*atideśa*) to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites.
[Reply: It is said: because even those things lacking a qualification are not different in their status as effects (*kāryatva*).
Furthermore, because the means [of cognition] has not yet been established, the inquiry as to "how" is indeed appropriate.
This introduces the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) according to the view of the Bhaṭṭas.
[Objection: But in that case, you have admitted the existence of an intermediate context.
For it is the established doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas that "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is the expectancy as to "how" a duty is to be performed.
[Objection: This excludes intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). [Response: There is no such thing as "intermediate context" that exists as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because when the object of cognition is absent, the means of valid cognition cannot be established;

for as long as those intermediate apūrvas are not understood, the entire collection of constituent elements that provide indirect assistance is, without distinction, encompassed by the injunction of the primary rite.

But subsequently, since there is no distinction in all [the rites] entering into the sphere of eligibility (*adhikāra*), they do not exist for one another's sake; thus, it is impossible for them to be applied by means of a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).
However, as for those [subsidiary acts] which are established by means of sentences and so forth,
the intermediate apūrvas are placed within them; being firmly rooted there, they will not transfer to the supreme apūrva.
An objection: "In that case, would it not follow that the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Soma sacrifice applies to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth?
This is not a fault.
For if there were an intrinsic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) even for those [rites] lacking a specific qualification, just as there is for those possessing one, [then this consequence would indeed follow].
It might be so;
however, because it is not something to be performed, there is no inherent requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). But how, then, can there be the status of being an effect (*kāryatā*)?
And [there would be] the impossibility of its being performed;
the refutation of that is as follows: "Surely you have never heard the seventh [chapter] before!
For it was clearly stated there by the Teacher: 'That very thing which is understood by a person independently as "this is my duty to do" [is what prompts action]. "
That [which is already established] is to be performed;
however, that which is not yet established and is employed for the sake of accomplishing that [performance] is the "task" (kārya).
And the supreme apūrva is understood as a task that is independent.

For it is from the comprehension of the task (*kārya*) that the comprehension of the fruit (*phala*) arises, not from the comprehension of the fruit that the task arises; this has been thoroughly established in the first section of the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhādya*).
Therefore, the distinction between the accomplished (*siddha*) and the task to be performed (*anuṣṭheya-kārya*) is proven.
The production of the *apūrva* occurs in the context of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth;
for the expectancy as to "how" (*katham*) arises only regarding that which is to be performed,
not regarding the mere fact of something being an effect (*kārya*).

"In that case, there would be an extension (atideśa) of the *prayāja* and other elements into the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites by way of suppressing their expectancy, just as [the *prayāja*s] are suppressed in the *avahīna* sacrifice.
You have not correctly understood our position.
For this is our established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): there is no natural expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) in those [rites] that lack a specific qualification (*niradhikāra*)."
However, an expectancy arising from another cause is not denied.

In that regard, in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other such rites, an expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is postulated by observing the presence of the *prayāja* and other elements. Even for that which is naturally devoid of expectancy, an expectancy based on the intervention of another cause is indeed appropriate.
For example, even though the two words “the cloth comes into being” (*paṭo bhavati*) are syntactically complete, the utterance of the word “red” (*rakta*) creates an expectancy for [the quality] red;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) in the sentence “the red cloth comes into being.
Likewise, in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, there is no cause whatsoever that gives rise to such an expectancy.
There is no extension of the *saumika* (soma-related) rules [to the *iṣṭi*],
and it is established that the concluding ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *iṣṭi* applies to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites.

As for those who, by accepting the principle of "qualification based on qualification" (*adhikṛtādhikāra*), assert that the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries possess their own independent qualification (*sādhikāratā*):

In their case, regarding the *prayāja* and other such rites, by the principle of the *rātrisatra*, it follows that only one who desires the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would be entitled [to perform them];
thus, there is no possibility of a "qualified qualification" (*adhikṛtādhikāra*).
It might be argued: "The expectation for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) of the primary injunction is not fulfilled."
Let there be no fulfillment [of the injunction];

for the words of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) fall within the scope of authoritative means of knowledge, and it is not the case that their function is beyond perception; therefore, it is appropriate that only one who desires the fruit to be established by them is the qualified person (*adhikārī*).

However, because they are understood as being for the sake of that [principal rite] merely by virtue of their proximity to a rule possessing an entitlement (*sādhikāra-vidhi*), there is no requirement for an entitlement (*adhikārākāṅkṣā*) for those [subsidiary rules] that lack an entitlement themselves; thus, the words of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) terminate solely in being explanatory passages.
Likewise, in cases such as "Milk is the vow for a Brāhmaṇa" (*payo vrataṃ brāhmaṇasya*), it is like the restriction regarding the acquisition of materials for one who has already set out to eat.
Since the qualified performer is already obtained within its own sentence (*svavākya*), it is not possible to assume a qualification for one who has entered into the primary context (*pradhāna*).
Otherwise, independence (*svātantrya*) would result for the milk-vow (*payovrata*) and other such observances.

Likewise, although the injunction "one shall not speak untruth" (*nānṛtaṃ vadet*) is studied within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), since the qualification of the agent of the prohibited action is understood from that very sentence, there is no possibility of its entry into the context.

Likewise, in the case of the injunction "he offers when [the vessel] is broken," because the occasion (*nimitta*) serves as a qualification of the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*), the offering cannot be established as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices unless that occasion is postulated; for without it, no specific person entitled to the rite could be identified. However, this is not the resolution here, because the word "broken" (*bhinna*) is etymological (*yaugika*) and thus refers back to the subject matter at hand.

Even for one who possesses the indicative mark (*nimitta*), there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) for that which is already entitled, because within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), that which is distinct is not employed;
for that [distinct element] is merely proximate within the context.
That which has been enjoined therein cannot be enjoined for something else that is distinct;
moreover, when there is a requirement for a qualification and one has begun to postulate a qualification, [the injunction must apply to that].
Why should an entitlement be postulated on the basis of proximity [of meaning] when the word expressing entitlement is directly heard?
For when the word expressing entitlement is heard in the principal sentence, it becomes connected with the principal [act].

The fundamental argument for refuting *anuṣaṅga* (syntactic ellipsis) is that there is no expectancy for a governing injunction (*adhikāra*) in the case of those [sentences] that are proximate, have not been heard as having a governing context, and are already connected to a governing purpose through their own specific purposes. However, it is merely a secondary point that it would be better to satisfy the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) through *anuṣaṅga*.
This concludes the discussion on the doubt regarding the optionality of the *prayāja* offerings and its resolution.

Moreover, in each instance of such injunctions as "He offers the *samidh* [oblation]" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 2.6.1.1), since it is understood that the person authorized is one already engaged in the primary sacrifice, the *samidh* and other rites individually constitute the means to the primary sacrifice; consequently, there would be a separate set of procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) for each.

For in that case, the intermediate injunctions (*avāntara-vidhi*) establish the status of their respective objects as means, because it is impossible for them to possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatā*) toward the supreme unseen potency (*paramāpūrva*), which is already occupied by the primary instrument.
The status of being a means is conceived solely on the basis of producing an assistance for the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Consequently, since they are accepted as independent means, and because each one individually accomplishes an assistance for the instrument, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) among the *samidh* and other materials.

However, when the prescriptive rule of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) grasps them merely as being for that purpose, it cannot otherwise be established unless they are connected with that [instrument].

In order to establish that purpose, one must postulate the production of an auxiliary function by the instrument; and that [function] follows the positive concomitance (anvaya). Furthermore, in the case of positive concomitance, all [factors] occur simultaneously.

In that regard, if each [cause] were to produce the auxiliary benefit for the instrument individually, then in the case of an option (vikalpa), the concomitance would not be established as if it were constant; however, if one accepts that the production of that benefit belongs to them when combined, then the concomitance is established in every respect.
It is not that there is an absence of procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for each [individual means] separately.

However, since there exists a relationship between the means and the goal, and because the status of being a means is optional when they are connected for the sake of that [goal], it is logical that their connection occurs in exactly that manner.

There is a doubt regarding the extension (*atideśa*) of the *saumika* (Soma-sacrifice) details to the *prayāja* offerings and others. Furthermore, since all [rites] possess a qualification (*sādhikāra*) by virtue of being subordinate to a primary qualified act (*adhikṛtādhikāra*),
the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) in the case of the *prayāja* and other such elements is inherent.
The extension of the *saumika* (Soma-related) ritual properties should apply to them;
nor should it be argued that, despite the existence of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), there is no extension of *saumika* properties to them due to circularity (*itaretarāśrayatā*).
For Soma possesses subsidiaries such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, and the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are recipients of the *aiṣṭika* (sacrificial) properties.
If the characteristics of the Soma sacrifice were to apply even to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth,
then there would be a very clear case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
This is the refutation thereof.
This is merely the prattle of the ignorant.

Just as in the case of the Soma sacrifice, even without the acquisition of the ritual details (dharma) pertaining to the iṣṭi, the benefit arises solely based on the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other such rites; likewise, in the case of the iṣṭi as well, the benefit occurs independently of the ritual details pertaining to the Soma sacrifice.
At most, the two subsidiaries (aṅgas) may receive assistance from the two [principal acts],
yet there is no fault whatsoever, because there is no contradiction in the conceptualization of assistance in that case.
In the case of subsidiaries that lack a specific qualification (niradhikāra), there is no inherent expectancy for a procedure (itikartavyatākāṅkṣā).
However, it was shown at the outset that [the application] arises from the force of indicative power (*liṅga*).
Therefore, since there is no arising of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in those things lacking indicative power,
there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the Soma-related ritual properties (*saumika-dharma*) to the *prayāja* offerings and the like.

Some raise an objection: "If the entry into the context of the subject matter (*prakṛta*) does not occur merely by virtue of being mentioned in proximity (*sannidhi*), then even the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, which is mentioned within the context of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, would—according to the rule ‘it is taken on the second day of a two-night sacrifice’—be considered merely a modification (*vaikṛta*).
This is the refutation of that objection.
That is incorrect.
This injunction regarding the taking [of the substance] depends upon that which is to be taken;
therein, by virtue of being the subject under discussion, it is the *soma* juice alone that connects as the object to be taken.
And since that [injunction] is connected to the qualification for the Jyotiṣṭoma, its inclusion therein is established;
subsequently, however, its connection with the Dvirātra is again made by means of a syntactical statement (vākya), so there is nothing inconsistent about this.
Thus, regarding the *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly contributing) elements, which are first connected to the mandate of qualification (*adhikāraniyoga*) by virtue of being for its sake (*tādarthya*),

there arises the postulation of their causality through the mandate of qualification— which has not yet been perceived— since the production of the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*) is not otherwise understood by means of the qualified injunction (*sādhikāro vidhiḥ*) as something to be performed.

Furthermore, since these momentary elements cannot produce assistance collectively in their own essential forms (*svarūpa*) because they do not exist simultaneously with one another, intermediate transcendental potencies (*avāntarāpūrva*) are accepted.
1443. An objection regarding the basis of the action (*āśrayikarma*) according to the Bhaṭṭa school:

"In that case, since even in the absence of an *apūrva*, the production of assistance for the instrument (*karaṇa*) can be established through the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the substance and the deity in the case of actions based on a substrate (*āśrayikarma*), there is no evidence whatsoever for resorting to an *apūrva*.
The resolution according to the Prābhākara school:
Are you perhaps inattentive regarding the *Ṛjuvimalā*?

For it has been shown there, in the fourth [chapter], that there is no direct benefit to the substance or the deity in the sacrifice; rather, [it occurs] through the medium of the portions consisting of the mantras and so forth, which constitute its own constituent parts (*svāṅga*).
Furthermore, as long as the sacrifice has not entered into the sphere of the person's qualification (adhikāra), the application (viniyoga) of those two [the subsidiary acts] to it is not possible;
nor can the sacrifice enter into the sphere of qualification without the *apūrva*. Therefore, an intermediate *apūrva* must necessarily be admitted.
And since these [intermediate *apūrvas*] are unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*), they do not possess the capacity to motivate action (*prayojakatva*).
And because it is directly perceived, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the substance and the deity alone is the motivator [of the action].
Even there, between the refinement of the substance and the deity, it should be understood that the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the substance is the sole motivator,
since the substance functions directly in the sacrifice.
However, there is no application of a substance through direct scriptural statement (śruti);
scripture nowhere provides a means for a substance,
nor is there an application of a substance even by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa).
Because it lacks the capacity to produce assistance toward direct realization;
for that [realization] indeed arises through an inferential mark (liṅga) or a scriptural statement (vākya).
Whether by position (sthāna) or by name (samākhyā), the connection with the productive meaning (bhāvārtha) alone exists as the cause of generation;
however, the application of qualities (guṇa) and classes (jāti) occurs through syntactical connection (vākya).
Because the instruments have various distinct functions,
when a substance that serves as a means is taken up, the two [the genus and the quality] are indeed useful as delimiters of that substance; thus,
their application as *kārakas* (factors of action) is not contradicted.
The determination of practice by means of the number associated with the arisen action:
that which is the number inherent in the arisen action—
for example, "He performs eleven *prayāja* offerings" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 3.6.5.1).
Since it is impossible to perform a ritual for actions that have already arisen, the rite is prescribed as being dependent upon the action.

Furthermore, although a qualification attached to the subject of a statement cannot be intended [as significant] for fear of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*), the collective performance (*sāhitya*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is not intended to be significant.
Nevertheless, because it is established as distinct [from each individual], there is no connection with each one separately,
but rather only with the collection as a whole;
and its fulfillment does not occur without repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

By implication, when resorting to repetition (*abhyāsa*), the fulfillment [of the required number] occurs precisely through an expansion in its own place (*svasthāna-vivṛddhi*) due to the inclusion of the subject at hand.
Furthermore, that quality (*guṇa*) called "number" which is inherent in the action being produced is not something to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
For it delimits the actions that are being enjoined; yet it is not possible for it itself to be an object of injunction.
Since an accumulation is indeed obtained when many things are enjoined, it does not assume the status of a separate object of injunction.
Moreover, even though it is not something that can be directly enjoined, it assists in the injunction by qualifying the meaning of the verbal root; thus, it is the correlative element.
However, that which is denoted by a distinct nominal stem is enjoined as a factor (kāraka) toward the ritual action, just like the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) and so forth.
The determination of the status of the singularity of the animal as a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) based on its material cause (*upādāna*):

Furthermore, although this [singularity], which is denoted by the case-ending (*vibhakti*), has a connection with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by virtue of its own power, [it is nevertheless subordinate].
Nevertheless, since its connection with that [substance] alone would not justify a connection with the *grāhaka* (the appropriating agent) established by the context (*prakaraṇa*),
it is determined that the connection with the state of being the *grāhaka* is indeed based on the act of appropriation (*aupādānika*).
For the appropriation of an animal or the like, which has already been assigned [to a specific rite], is not possible unless it is specifically delimited.
There is a requirement for the number that serves as its delimiting factor, and since a number requires a substratum to fulfill its connection with the perceived subject,
the injunction (vidhi) postulates its relation to that state.
The injunctive meaning, being associated with a number, is understood; for the sake of establishing its connection, it brings about a relation to the state of the apprehender (*grāhakīyadaśā*).
This is the presentation of the object of the undertaking (*upādāna*).
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the function of the injunction characterized as "undertaking" (*upādānalakṣaṇa*) is synonymous with "implication" (*ākṣepa*).
The subject matter consists of origination (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), entitlement (*adhikāra*), and performance (*prayoga*).
And the very impossibility of the injunction as it is perceived is the seed [of this inquiry].
In such cases as "One should offer a cake to Sūrya," the injunction understood as involving an entitlement is untenable without an origination; therefore, it implies an origination.
For it has been stated many times that a mere momentary sacrifice, independent of the injunction for its production, is not capable of establishing entitlement;
therefore, that very [injunction] is the seed for the conceptualization of entitlement in the case of the Viśvajit and other such rites.

Furthermore, when the entitlement is contingent upon a specific occasion (nimitta), the injunction, existing as the goal to be accomplished, implies the performance of the means, which is synonymous with execution.

Regarding the section on desire (*kāmādhikāra*), however, because the accomplishment of desire depends upon that [desire], mental activity is already dependent on the fruit even before the performance of the ritual act; thus, since there is no obstacle, an injunction (*vidhi*) is not the motivator. In both cases, with respect to the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*), the sacrifice itself (*kratu*) alone is the motivator.
This is because they serve as the means for assisting the ritual acts;
for whatever is the effect of something, that alone is its motivator.

The function of the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) is to assist the ritual intention (*kratu*); that alone is the cause for their performance. And whatever is implied by an injunction (*vidhi*) for the sake of its own accomplishment—
"Therefore, it is that which is to be enjoined"—this is the conventional usage in the *Tantra*.
[Objection: If this were so, then even the qualification (*adhikāra*) in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others would necessarily be something to be enjoined by virtue of being implied.
[Reply: It is said in response:
The qualification has no function in the accomplishment of the injunction,
but rather in [establishing] agency; and the implication of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is for the purpose of understanding that [agency].
According to the Vivaraṇa, there is no presentation of the sequence as being denoted by words.

And thus—the Mīmāṃsakas' outburst is that "sequence is not something to be enjoined (vidheya), because it is not implied for the sake of the injunction's own establishment. Regarding the determination of the Nibandhana's view: there is no denotation whatsoever of the sequence belonging to the fifth [book].

Furthermore, for that which has not been expressed [as a subordinate], neither a status of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) based on injunction (*viniyogika*) nor one based on material requirement (*aupādānika*) is possible; nor does an injunction have the power to imply that which has not become a subsidiary.

As for the sequence denoted by the word "first" in the rule [Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 12.24.6], "The first portion belongs to the one who utters 'vaṣaṭ'," the author of the Nibandhana states that this sequence is indeed subject to application and is something to be enjoined.
For this very reason, it is considered in the third [section].

Indeed, regarding the sequence of hearing (*śrautakrama*) found in the fifth [section], such as "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati... (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 12.1.1.10) and so forth, there is no explicit statement (*abhidhāna*) concerning it.
How, then, is it understood?
For although the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed after a verbal root when the agent is the same [for both actions],
it is that which is employed first [that is understood as the primary action].
It is prescribed from that very [source],
because the suffix *ktvā* is heard there;
likewise, the understanding of the meaning regarding the state of being employed first is also exactly so.
Since the comprehension of the meaning arises from the manner in which it was practiced, and since the performance follows that comprehension,
the sequence of that [performance] is likewise understood to be of that very same kind.
An examination of the non-sequential expression of meaning and so forth [is as follows]:
1457. Regarding meaning and the rest, any suspicion that they are directly expressed is cast far aside.
Furthermore, the fact that even that which is not directly expressed serves as a means for comprehension has already been considered in various contexts.
Regarding the objection and resolution concerning the fact that sequence is characterized by scriptural injunction (*codanā*):
if sequence does not possess subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) with respect to the meaning of the injunction, how then can it be characterized by scriptural injunction?
Subservience (*vidheyatā*) is not the reason for being characterized by injunction (*codanālakṣaṇatva*),

because it would follow that the qualification (*adhikāra*) lacks that status. Rather, the fact that the meaning of the injunction, conjoined with that [qualification], is what is to be established constitutes being characterized by injunction.

In that case, since the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*) is also determined as being endowed with a sequence, its status as being characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanālakṣaṇatva*) is not contradictory;
for the injunction regarding performance is understood as being delimited by a performance embraced by a specific sequence.
For this very reason, although sequence is not an integral part [of the sacrifice], it is nevertheless respected,
because in its absence the performance would be impossible, and because the injunction of performance must be accomplished through a qualified performance.
Thus, the instructional [knowledge] is of two kinds: that which is based on application and that which is based on material cause.
This concludes the determination of the subject matter.
In that case, the application (viniyoga) is not determined according to the qualification (adhikāra), but rather the qualification is determined according to the application;
for the application is established even by resorting to a qualification in a general sense.
Although, for the sake of establishing the fixed application (*viniyoga*) in each specific section, there must first be a grasping (*grahaṇa*) by a grasper (*grāhaka*),

and although only that which possesses a mandate (*sādhikāra*) can be a grasper, nevertheless, when a general agent of qualification (*adhikārin*) such as "one who desires heaven" is found, the state of possessing a mandate is thereby accomplished.

When the apprehension of the agent (*grāhaka*) has occurred and the constituent parts (*aṅga*) have been assigned, there arises the entitlement (*adhikāra*) of one who desires heaven and is capable of performing that [rite]—namely, the mandate (*vidhi*) whose nature is a task (*kārya*) as delimited by those parts; subsequently, there follows the restriction regarding the specific qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaniyama*).
For this very reason, in the case of those who possess the constituent parts such as looking, hearing, and stepping forward, the blind, the deaf, the lame, and so forth [are excluded].

Those who have not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) lack the qualification for [rites] that possess as their constituent parts the selection of three ancestral sages (ārṣeya-traya-varaṇa)— as in the case of those for whom no such sages exist— and for those involving the Āhavanīya and other fires;
this is because they lack the natural capacity to fulfill the purpose of such injunctions, as one should infer for oneself.
The description of eligibility is given by means of remedying the deficiencies of limbs for those who are incapable, and by the acquisition of wealth for those who lack it;
however, for those whose innate capacity is not departed, [there is no such requirement].

1462. It is indeed the case that those who lack the requisite material wealth possess the qualification [for ritual action]; however, is it not true that their qualification cannot be established at all, since that [qualification] is contingent upon the accomplishment of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency)?
True; because it depends upon the entire collection of her limbs,
it certainly does not fall within the scope of desire.
This is because that [action] has as its object the efficient-force (bhāvanā) which possesses both the procedure (itikartavyatā) and the fruit;
for it is not possible for one who desires a fruit to have the qualification (adhikāra) with respect to an efficient-force toward which the action has not become the instrument (karaṇa).
And it is generally accepted that every instrument attains the status of being an instrument only when accompanied by its procedure.
Consequently, if the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are not performed, the requirement of performing them along with their attendant procedures (*setikartavyatākatva*) is contradicted;

and since the object (*viṣaya*) [of the injunction] is absent, the subject (*viṣayin*) [the person entitled to it] cannot logically exist, resulting in the total collapse of the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for those desiring results.
Regarding the auxiliaries in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), the principle of "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti-nyāya*) applies.

Furthermore, for one who possesses the causal signs (*nimittavat*), the qualification (*adhikāra*) pertains solely to the objective of the essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*). Thus, even when the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are not fully assembled, because the object is not lost from view, there is no loss of the understanding of qualification. Moreover, that unimpaired qualification only then makes known the necessity of accomplishing it through the assembly of all the auxiliaries that are to be assembled;
however, the general rule is indeed that its accomplishment depends upon the totality of the auxiliaries.

With this very intention, the Prābhākaras’ boastful claim is that, within the context of the occasioning causes (*nimitta*), the meaning of the scripture is both secondary (*gauṇa*) and primary (*mukhya*).
The performance of occasional rites (*naimittika*) is merely occasional.
And there is the statement that "the repetition occurs for every individual cause.
Furthermore, there are certain subsidiary elements whose performance depends upon a specific cause;
such an element exists only when that cause is present.
For example: “He offers when [the ladle] has broken.

In this case, the meaning of the scriptural injunction is as follows: when a breakage occurs, the collection of subsidiary elements accompanied by the offering for breakage produces the assistance for the performance; however, in its absence, the collection of subsidiaries alone does so.
As long as the process beginning with the breaking [of the vessel] recurs,
for that long the oblation (homa) is repeated. This much, then, is the collection of subsidiary elements (aṅgakalāpa) taught by the Upaniṣads.
The commencement of the investigation into the performance of the ritual action (*kāryaprayoga*).

The Mīmāṃsakas consider certain auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to be based upon the ritual action (*kāryanibandhana*). For the instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding the auxiliaries is indeed established according to each specific section (*prakaraṇa*).
Because the application [of a ritual act] is preceded by the apprehension of what was not previously known.

For if the injunction regarding the *samit* and other offerings— namely, “he offers the *samit*”— were intended as a prescription for the sacrifice with its specific qualification (the desire for heaven) by means of the statement, “one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices,” then, because it would be prescribed with reference to that [sacrifice], [the injunction would be subordinate].
If the injunction regarding the *samit* and other materials were merely for the sake of the sacrifice itself,
then because the *samit* and others would be enjoined in all sacrifices that involve a *yaji*, the instruction would not be restricted;
for in that case, the term "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) would not apply.

Alternatively, the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* is sufficient as a qualifier; for if one intended to express a qualifier of that which is being pointed out (*uddiśyamāna*), it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

However, since the expression "by means of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*" constitutes the sentence of entitlement (*adhikāravākya*), the denotation of the related meaning is established through mere proximity (*sannidhāna*) alone.

Since the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and other subsidiaries enter into that [apūrva], their performance is accomplished through their application to that specific purpose; therefore, the injunctive sentence regarding qualification, "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām*), does not itself provide the object to be aimed at (*uddeśya*).
In that context, there is an *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related) of the subsidiaries with the *apūrva*, by virtue of their being for its sake (*tādarthya*).
And by means of the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is the conceptualization of the door characterized as the assistance rendered by the instrument (*karaṇa*).
