Therein, through the operation of injunction (*vidhi*) characterized as appropriation (*upādāna*), there is the conceptualization of the collective accessories (*aṅga*) as being generators of assistance; thus is the determination of the accessories for each respective context.
The determination of the object of action (*kārya*) as the means of knowledge. But where, and for whom, does subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) based on the effect (*kārya*) apply?
It applies to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements in relation to the modified apūrvas (*vaikṛtāpūrva*).
And regarding its performance, they declare this extension (*atideśa*):
when original elements fall from their original positions into another purpose, that which they designate as *ūha*.
Verbal [knowledge] is of two kinds: that which arises from instruction, and [that which arises from inference].

In that context, once the efficient force (*bhāvārtha*)—which is the object of the modified *apūrva* (the end to be accomplished) that requires both the instrument and its procedure—has been established as the instrument, there remains a further requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
And in that case, it is not possible to postulate another auxiliary function as one does for the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).

For once another auxiliary function has been postulated, the subsequent requirement for two types of entities capable of producing it cannot be fulfilled by a connection with the group of items studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*).
However, when the archetypal auxiliary function is accepted, [the requirement is satisfied].
Since the requirement for expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is fulfilled by the presentation of the two types of archetypal objects through that [archetype],
it adopts only the archetypal auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*).
This concludes the determination that inference and analogy, as favored by the Bhāṭṭas, are not causes for extended application (*atideśa*).
What, then, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its acceptance? It is not inference (*anumāna*), because there is an absence of an unerring relationship with a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Nor is it analogy (*upamāna*), because that has as its object merely similarity.
Furthermore, since these two [means of knowledge], which penetrate established objects, do not apply their authority to the result [of action],
the verbal suffix *liṅ* and so forth denote the "natural benefit" (*prākṛtopakāra*).
This is what is said.

That very word, such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which denotes an injunction (*niyoga*), expresses its own meaning as conjoined with the assistance provided by the archetypal ritual (*prakṛta*). It expresses its own meaning as conjoined with the assistance provided by the archetypal ritual.

Even in the case of the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers express their own meaning as connected with the assistance (*upakāra*) postulated for the sake of the injunction;
and in the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhi*) are the causes [of such connection].
Here, at least, there is no dispute regarding the expectancy and compatibility of the archetypal assistance itself.

As for "proximity" (*sannidhāna*), it is by means of the original (*prākṛta*) and the unprecedented (*apūrva*) specific indicative mark (*liṅga-viśeṣaṇa*) that the original and the unprecedented are brought into proximity within the intellect;
and that [unprecedented element] brings along its own auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*).
For this very reason, the knowers of reality (*tattvavidaḥ*) maintain that the connection with the auxiliary benefit is based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*).
The presentation of the fact that assistance [rendered] in a modified sacrifice (vikṛti) is based on direct injunction (aupadeśika):
for that which is presented by the text or by the meaning of an injunction enters into syntactic connection with it.
That is based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*),
such as the benefit in the archetype (*prakṛti*),
or, for example, the eligibility in the Viśvajit and other sacrifices.

Thus, once the assistance (*upakāra*) has entered into a relationship [with the sacrifice], there arises a doubt as to which group of ritual items (*padārtha-varga*) produces that very modified *apūrva*. Now, one might object: since in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) that assistance is already known to have its producing group of items established, there is no cause for the arising of such an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
For this very reason, they maintain that there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the constituent elements (*padārtha*).

If there were a subsequent expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) even regarding the constituent elements themselves, then— given that such expectancy is the cause for the connection of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements with the modified (*vaikṛta*) apūrva— [extension would indeed occur].
Who indeed would prevent the extension (*atideśa*) of the meaning of words, just as one prevents the extension of a benefit?
For those who know the doctrine of extension maintain that "extension is the connection with something else of what has been stated elsewhere.
This is its refutation.

To this we reply: if the primary ritual elements were prompted by the assistance rendered to the instruments (*karaṇa*), then once those generators (*janaka*) were fully known, the expectation for the principal act (*pradhāna*) would not arise.
However, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the ritual properties (*dharma*) are prompted by the *apūrva*.
That being the case, those ritual elements (dharmas) are prompted by the *apūrva*;
their capacity to produce is postulated only with respect to an assistance (*upakāra*) connected to that [specific *apūrva*],
not to one connected to anything else.
Therefore, it is not untenable that the modified *apūrva* (transformational transcendental result), whose means have not yet been ascertained, possesses a requirement for those means.
However, for those constituent elements (*padārtha*) whose status as means has already been established, there is merely their performance;
since their status as means for the benefit [of the sacrifice] is based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*), there would be no need for modification (*ūha*) or annulment (*bādha*).
However, regarding the connection with the *apūrva* of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) based on expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), we shall explain how the aforementioned understandings are established.

And this being so, when there is an expectancy for constituent elements (*padārtha*), those archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements subsequently come to be objects of the intellect by means of their contribution (*upakāra*).
They attain the subsequent [cognition].
This is the presentation of how assistance brings about the presence of ordinary objects.
But by what connection does assistance bring them to mind?
It is said:
in the original model (prakṛti), the relationship between those constituent elements (padārtha) and that assistance (upakāra) is understood as one of produced and producer (janya-janakabhāva).
Through that prior cognition, memory arises regarding them.

When they are present in memory and their mutual connection has been established—as they were studied according to the context—then subsequently, the status of being a means to the benefit (*upakāra*) is postulated for them when combined.

As they have said: "The ritual procedure (*vidhi*), having first presented the group of modified items (*vaikṛta*) with the archetypal benefits (*prākṛta-upakāra*), then postulates the means by unifying them within the benefit."

Furthermore, the verbal cognition that arises from the connection with ordinary objects presented by the effect characterized as "assistance" (upakāra) is called verbal [cognition] born from the effect of the modified apūrva.
Nor is it untenable for words to have a connection with a distinct apūrva, because there is no relation of one thing to another that belongs to something else. (Bṛhat-Ṭīkā 10.1.1).
And this point has been thoroughly discussed in the *Kṛtju*, *Vimala*, and other works.
This is the determination of the verbal nature of *ūha* (modification).

In that regard, the determination of the connection between archetypal (*prākṛta*) ritual refinements (*saṃskāra*) and those ritual items (*padārtha*) which occupy the place of the archetypal substances—though it is also known by the name *ūha*—is indeed verbal (*śābda*), as it arises from the [scriptural] injunction (*kāryaja*).

When there is the certainty that "this is indeed that very same [act]," regarding the function of threshing and so forth as it was recognized in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), there follows the determination of their connection with another substance belonging to the modified rite (*vaikṛta*).
Since threshing and other such acts have an unseen purpose (*apūrva*),

the meaning of the scriptural injunction in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is that the raw material which produces the rice grains belonging to that [sacrifice] must be consecrated by threshing and the like.
In the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well, wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like are of the same nature.

The determination of sublation (*bādha*). Thus, when threshing and other such acts are inferred for black gram (*kṛṣṇala*) and the like, the certainty of sublation— which arises because of the absence of the purpose that serves as the gateway—
is also produced solely by that purpose.

Thus it is established that the ordinary (*prākṛta*) auxiliary benefit arises from constituent elements (*padārtha*) that have been modified (*ūhita*), sublated (*bādhitā*), or augmented (*abhyucita*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
This concludes the examination of *tantra* (common performance) and *āvāpa* (repetition).

Regarding those auxiliaries (*aṅga*) which are directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) and connected to their specific functions, when they relate to multiple primary acts (*pradhāna*), the specific application (*prayukti-viśeṣa*) of their performance is called *tantra*.
Likewise, when there is no difference in the effect itself, no distinction is perceived among the place, time, and agent, which constitute the adjuncts (*anubandha*) of the performance (*prayoga*).
However, when the effect differs, the performance must indeed be repeated for the sake of that effect;
for even when there is a difference in place and so forth, since a difference in the performance is understood, there is necessarily a repetition of the performance.
An examination of the incidental application (*prasaṅga*):

When it is understood that the performance of something, even though carried out for the sake of another, has its own independent purpose, then since it is likewise beneficial in other instances as well, there is a single performance [of that act]. Thus it is concluded.
This conduct is the means for reaching the further shore of those [teachings] that are vast and profound. // 1 //

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Auxiliary Factors that Contribute Remotely," within the *Aṅgapārāyaṇa* section of the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor (Mahāmahopādhyāya) Śrīmacchālikanātha Miśra.
